Hi,

Thank you for creating this tool. It will help me a lot especially for me thesis.

I am trying to analyse single sample LNCaP data. My aim is to find compare transcription factor methylation levels. To compare TF methylation levels I thought using segmentation analysis could be useful.

In short, I created my granges object that contains bed intervals like in the segmentation example. I get negative width interval and I literally checked the mean and sd of my peaks to be sure about end is greater than start.


To sum up,

- Is my intent correct ? Can I use segmentation method for my aim?
- If so, what could be my mistake to get that error. I would be more than happy if you could troubleshoot my problem.

Best regards,

Tunc.

I am trying to analyse single sample LNCaP data. My aim is to find compare transcription factor methylation levels. To compare TF methylation levels I thought using segmentation analysis could be useful.

I assume you want to analyze methylation levels on transcription factor binding sites not transcription factors. If so, this is not the best way to do this. If you know where the sites are simply calculate mean methylation levels on and around them. You can do this via genomation package: https://www.r-bloggers.com/using-genomation-to-analyze-methylation-profiles-from-roadmap-epigenomics-and-encode/

In short, I created my granges object that contains bed intervals like in the segmentation example. I get negative width interval and I literally checked the mean and sd of my peaks to be sure about end is greater than start.
Please send a reproducible example.

To sum up,

- Is my intent correct ? Can I use segmentation method for my aim?
I would do as I described above, segmentation may not work. low methylation segments can harbour multiple binding sites. No clear way to assign them to distinct sites.
- If so, what could be my mistake to get that error. I would be more than happy if you could troubleshoot my problem.
I can't tell what is wrong with your code or data. Please send a reproducible example, if you want to pursue segmentation further.

Best regards,

Tunc.

messages.subject: Re: MethSeg() negative widths are not allowed error.
parts:
Hi,

Thank you for answering and spending time on my question.

https://www.dropbox.com/s/igv1rlcn3act2m8/sample1.bed?dl=0 —> This is the "bed" like methylation data from ENCODE RRBS. It is first 10k lines.
https://www.dropbox.com/s/240k2u1v5qzdch0/sample1.RData?dl=0 —> This is the granges object that I try to feed in methSeg() function and get the following error. I shared that newmeth object that I created with the following code.

myfile <- read.table('/Users/morova/Desktop/methylation/sample1.bed',sep = '\t',stringsAsFactors = F)
newmeth <- GRanges(seqnames = Rle(myfile[,"V1"]),ranges = IRanges(start = myfile[,"V2"],width = 1),
                   score = myfile[,"V11"]/100)
res=methSeg(newmeth,diagnostic.plot=TRUE,maxInt=100,minSeg=10)

This one is from tutorial which influenced me for trying methSegment.
In the context of methylation, we first extract segments between change points of the signal (methylation profiles) then cluster those segments into groups based on the mean methylation values of the segments. In this case, a segment is a region of the genome where CpGs have similar methylation values. We cluster those segments into segment groups using mixture modeling. The segment groups correspond to highly methylated regions or lowly methylated regions. Since this is an unsupervised method, we can find more patterns than just highly or lowly methylated regions. The users have to further overlap the segments with other marks and annotation such as promoters, H3K27ac or other histone modifications to associate segment groups with functional annotation.

T.
